title: Immutability Helper
statement:
Write a class `ImmutableHelper` that produces edited copies of a JSON value while leaving the value itself untouched.

- `new ImmutableHelper(obj)` receives `obj`, a JSON object or array.
- `produce(mutator)` calls `mutator` once with a stand-in for `obj`. Through it the mutator reads and assigns properties, including those of nested objects and arrays, as if it were editing `obj`, and every read sees the assignments made before it. `produce` returns a new value: `obj` with all of those assignments applied. `obj` itself must never change, and every call starts again from the original `obj`.

Every mutator returns `undefined`, never reads a key that does not exist, never deletes keys and never calls methods such as `push`. It assigns only numbers, strings, booleans or `null`, never to a key that holds an object or array, and in an array only to an existing index or to the index equal to the length (which appends).

A JSON case cannot hold functions, so each mutator is written as a list of statements in a small part of JavaScript, which the judge turns into a function `proxy => { ... }` that runs them in order:

- `let name = e` keeps a value, or a reference to a nested object or array, in a new variable;
- `target = e`, `target += e` and `target -= e` assign to a property, where `target` is a variable followed by `.key` and `[index]` steps, such as `proxy.arr[0]` or `data.x`;
- an expression `e` is a number, a double-quoted string, `true`, `false`, `null`, or a variable followed by zero or more such steps; several of them may be joined by `+` and `-` (numbers only).

Each case gives `obj` and `mutators`. The judge creates `new ImmutableHelper(obj)` and calls `produce` once per mutator, in order. The answer is the list of returned values, compared regardless of the order of object keys. A solution that changes `obj` fails the case.
constraints: obj is a JSON object or array, and no key in it is "__proto__"
1 <= mutators.length < 10^5 (the total number of produce calls)
Each mutator is a list of at most 20 statements of at most 200 characters
Every mutator follows the rules above, and every number stays within ±2^53
api: class ImmutableHelper { constructor(obj: InputObj); produce(mutator: (obj: InputObj) => void): InputObj }, where InputObj is a JSON object or array
notes:
## Intuition

The simple way is to deep-copy `obj` for every call and let the mutator edit the copy, as the brute force does. That costs the size of `obj` per call, even when the mutator touches one number. A better plan is **copy-on-write**: hand the mutator a `Proxy` that only reads from `obj`, and make a shallow copy of a node the first time something in it is assigned. Every untouched subtree of the result is then the very same object as in `obj` (structural sharing), and `obj` is never written to.

## Approach

1. A *draft* wraps one node of `obj`: its `base`, a `copy` made on the first write, the drafts of the `children` read so far, and its `proxy`.
2. The `get` trap reads from `copy ?? base`. A primitive is returned as is; an object or array gets a child draft (made once and cached by key) and its proxy is returned, so the same path always leads to the same draft.
3. The `set` trap makes `copy` with a shallow spread if there is none yet, then assigns to it.
4. After the mutator, `finalize` works bottom up: a child whose result is still its `base` changed nothing; otherwise the parent gets a copy (if it has none) with that child replaced. A draft with no copy and no changed child returns its `base` unchanged.

## Example 1, step by step

`obj = { val: 10 }`.

- First call: `proxy.val += 1` reads `val` through `get` (10, a primitive), then `set` copies the root to `{ val: 10 }` and writes 11. `finalize` returns the copy `{ val: 11 }`.
- Second call: a fresh root draft reads 10 again, since `obj` was never written to, and returns `{ val: 9 }`.
- The answer is `[{ val: 11 }, { val: 9 }]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(R + W·k) per call for R reads and W writes, where k is the size of the nodes that get copied, instead of the size of `obj`.
- Space: the same: only copied nodes are new; everything else is shared with `obj`.

## Pitfalls

- Writing through to `obj` (or a shallow copy of only the root) changes the original's nested values.
- Making a new child draft on every read loses edits: in Example 3, `data` and later reads of `proxy.obj.val` must reach the same draft.
- A read after a write must see the new value, so `get` reads from `copy` when it exists.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `draft` | the edit state of one node: `base`, `copy`, `children`, `proxy` |
| `base` | the node of `obj` this draft stands for, never written to |
| `copy` | shallow copy of `base`, made on the first assignment |
| `children` | drafts of nested objects and arrays read so far, by key |
| `result` | what `finalize` returns for a draft |

narration.3: Keep a reference to obj; it is only ever read, never written.
narration.7: Every call starts with a fresh draft of the root of obj.
narration.8: The mutator edits through the root proxy and never touches obj directly.
narration.9: Build the result from the drafts that were read or written.
narration.13: A draft knows its original node, its copy (made on the first write), its child drafts and its proxy.
narration.16: Reads come from the copy once there is one, so they see earlier assignments.
narration.17: Numbers, strings, booleans and null are handed back as they are.
narration.18: A nested object or array gets one child draft per key, made on its first read and reused afterwards.
narration.19: Return the child proxy so assignments deeper down are caught as well.
narration.22: The first assignment to this node makes a shallow copy of it.
narration.23: Assign to the copy; the original node keeps its value.
narration.31: Start from this node's copy, or null if nothing was assigned directly to it.
narration.33: Finalize each child that was read, from the bottom up.
narration.34: An unchanged child stays shared with obj.
narration.35: A changed child forces a copy of its parent too, if it has none yet.
narration.38: With no changes at all, the original node itself is reused.
